source.title: Composer: A Search Framework for Hybrid Neural Architecture Design
source.authors: Bilge Acun; Prasoon Sinha; Newsha Ardalani; Sangmin Bae; Alicia Golden; Chien-Yu Lin; Meghana Madhyastha; Fei Sun; N. Yadwadkar; Carole-Jean Wu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or corruption.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation-loss outcomes across hybrid architectures and model sizes, and compares compute-scaling behavior, but does not reproduce the original power-law fitting method.
record.gate_note: The study cites Chinchilla scaling laws and reports its own architecture and scaling experiments. Results cited from prior work are not included as rows. Downstream task scores are reported, but the study does not test whether they are predictable from pretraining loss or scale.
record.test_reason: An architecture-search paper that compares many attention/MLP orderings and ratios at a fixed 1B parameter count under IsoFLOP budgets. Those DCLM validation-loss comparisons bear on V4 in a new setting: hybrid layer composition rather than depth or width. It does not fit power laws, extrapolate loss, report allocation exponents, or vary fitting choices. Its scaling-law use (Chinchilla IsoFLOP budgets, FLOP counting) is otherwise a tool.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Composer finds hybrid attention/MLP architectures (1:2 ratio, non-standard interleavings) that beat Llama 3.2 and prior hybrids in validation loss (headline 0.03), downstream accuracy (about 2% on average) and efficiency, from 350M to 8B. They show compute-optimal scaling similar to Llama, though validation at much larger scales remains open.
record.recipe_differences: The study searches and compares hybrid attention/MLP architectures and reports validation-loss and compute-scaling results; it does not fit the original studies' power laws or estimate parameter/token allocation exponents.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with search depth, primitive width scaling, dataset used for small-scale evaluation, stacking versus stretching extrapolation, and aggregation method. The paper reports that stretching performs better beyond 16-layer searches, while stacking works across search depths; width scaling reduces search cost by 6.38× and validation loss by 0.02-0.04.

fits_no_version.finding: Architecture rankings from tiny-scale search (400K-1M params) correlate with 1B-scale rankings (Spearman 0.97 and 0.9). Chinchilla-scaled-down DCLM search transferred poorly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small-scale architecture rankings can transfer to large scale, depending on proxy data and width-to-depth ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: The compute-optimal loss versus model size slope is nearly identical for hybrid and Llama architectures (-0.612 to -0.63) over 350M-3B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different attention/MLP compositions shift the scaling curve's offset but not its slope.

record.problems: The compute-optimal analysis reports only three slopes for validation loss versus model size, not fitted growth exponents for optimal parameters and tokens. Some scaling results are presented only in figures. The study states that larger-scale extrapolation (tens to hundreds of billions of parameters) needs further validation. The paper gives different loss-reduction summaries in different sections (0.05-1.0 across sizes and budgets, versus 0.03 for a fixed-token comparison).
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. Downstream-task accuracy results were not extracted because the paper reports benchmark performance, not a tested predictive relationship to pretraining loss or scale.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss against N, D or C. Sizes span only 350M-3B (8B for downstream tasks).
No loss extrapolation from fitted small-run laws; only architecture-ranking transfer.
Fig. 8 marks optimal model sizes per budget, but no N_opt or D_opt exponents are reported.
Depth versus width aspect ratio at fixed parameter count is not varied for the final models. Only attention/MLP ratio and ordering are varied.
Downstream accuracies are reported but not related to scale or loss predictively.
No analysis of fitting choices or setup effects on exponents.

missing.what: Validation losses of baseline architectures at 1B with 37.5B tokens: Llama 2.80, Sandwich 2.77, Striped 1:2/1:4/1:8 at 2.81/2.82/2.85, Composite 2.77 (stacked and stretched)
All-MLP p0 architecture has loss above 5 at 1B; all-attention p25 and attention-heavy p50/p100 perform worse
Stacking versus stretching losses across search depths 4-32 at 1B (e.g. stretched 10A+20M underperforms)
Optimal model size per compute budget (stars) for Llama and Composite models

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'challenges' label on V4 rests on R4's '0.05-1.0', which is very likely a typo; Table 2 and the abstract give 0.03. Even 0.05-0.1 is about 2-3% of loss, consistent with Kaplan's 'slight' range, so I dropped that challenge. Rows R1-R5 compare the study's own architectures with baselines; they are kept for V4 only as fixed-size architecture comparisons. R8-R10 are relinked to none.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss against parameters, tokens, or compute, nor a test of the power-law form across several orders of magnitude.
The study compares small- and large-scale architecture rankings, not power-law loss predictions fitted on small runs.

Figure 8 identifies optimal model sizes at compute budgets, and the text compares scaling behavior, but it does not report the parameter-count and token-count growth exponents or a fitted allocation trend.
Tests changes to computational-primitive ratios and interleavings, and width scaling; it does not systematically vary depth and width at fixed parameter count across a wide architecture range.
Experiments concern text pretraining; no other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling-law test.
Downstream accuracy is measured across sizes, but the study does not test whether it is predictable from pretraining loss or fit a downstream scaling relationship.
No study of how power-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation estimates change with fitting choices or setup.

conditions.value: width scaling versus no width scaling

rows.value: Validation loss reduces by 0.02-0.04 with width scaling
rows.note: The paper attributes the result to better preservation of width-to-depth characteristics during search; the compared search architectures differ as well as in width.
rows.check: Width scaling refers to search-time width only. Both final 1B models have Llama 3.2 1B width. The comparison is effectively 4x(2A+4M)+1A+2M versus 5x(3A+3M)+2A+2M at the same size, so it is an architecture-composition difference of 0.02-0.04 loss, not a width effect.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, Observation 5 and Figure 4-bottom discussion; Appendix B.4, Width Scaling.

rows.subject: Composite architectures (stacked and stretched; aggregate across sizes and budgets)
rows.operation_detail: Compared hybrid architectures with Llama 3.2 across model sizes and training budgets.
rows.value: Composite models consistently reduce loss by 0.05-1.0
rows.note: The paper also gives a 0.03 reduction in the abstract and for a separate fixed-token comparison in Section 4.3; this row records the Section 4.1 range as stated.
rows.check: The value '0.05-1.0' is almost certainly a typo (likely 0.05-0.1). Losses are about 2.8-3.2 (Fig. 5), and the abstract and Table 2 give 0.03. Fig. 5 covers 350M-3B; 8B appears only in downstream Table 6. This is the study's own method versus a baseline, and the magnitude cannot be read reliably.

relationships.condition: 1B models with the same width, varying attention/MLP ratio (roughly 1:1 to 1:2) and interleaving, under IsoFLOP or fixed-token budgets
relationships.reason: Loss differences between reasonable compositions are about 0.01-0.04 on a loss of about 2.8-3.0 (R1, R2, R3). Table 2 shows 2.77-2.85 across baselines (text-based; see missing).
relationships.display_finding: Reasonable compositions differed by about 0.01–0.04 at losses around 2.8–3.0, with baseline losses ranging from 2.77 to 2.85.

relationships.condition: Extreme primitive compositions at 1B: all-MLP, all-attention, or MLP-first orderings
relationships.reason: Text-based: the all-MLP p0 model has loss above 5, all-attention p25 'performs poorly', and MLP-first random architectures degrade. Composition outside a sensible range changes loss greatly (R5; see missing).
relationships.display_finding: The all-MLP model had loss above 5, the all-attention model performed poorly, and random architectures placing MLPs first also degraded.
